question: Should a Series B company hire a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer

For most Series B companies, hiring a fractional CRO is the right move when you need senior go-to-market leadership to install repeatable revenue process — but you either can't yet justify a $400K+ full-time package, or you haven't proven the exact profile the role requires. A fractional CRO gives you 15–25 hours a week of scar-tissue expertise to build the operating system, then hands it off to a full-time hire you'll be far better equipped to interview. The wrong move is using "fractional" as a permanent substitute for the owned, accountable leadership that a scaling revenue org eventually demands.

Series B is the awkward middle. You have product-market fit and a Series A war chest that's turned into real ARR, but the board just wired growth capital on the promise that revenue becomes a machine, not a founder's heroics. The question of whether to hire a fractional CRO is really a question about *sequencing*: what leadership does the next 12–18 months actually require, and how do you buy the expertise without overspending on a title you can't yet define? Below is the framework we use to answer it.

## What problem is a fractional CRO actually solving at Series B?

The instinct at Series B is to read "we need more revenue" as "we need a revenue leader," and to conflate that with "we need to hire a CRO." Those are three different statements. A fractional CRO is the correct answer to a specific one: *we have a go-to-market motion that works in flashes but isn't yet a system, and nobody on the team has built that system before.* If your founder or head of sales has already scaled a company from $5M to $50M ARR, you may not need one at all. If they haven't — which is the norm at Series B — you're asking a first-timer to build the hardest part of the company by trial and error, on the board's clock.

The fractional CRO's job is not to personally close deals. It's to install the revenue operating system: the segmentation and ICP discipline, the stage definitions and exit criteria in your pipeline, the comp plan that actually drives the behavior you want, the forecast cadence the board can trust, and the hiring scorecards for the reps and managers you're about to bring on. This is architecture work, and it's front-loaded. Much of the value lands in the first 90–120 days, which is precisely why a fractional engagement — dense senior time for a defined window — often fits the shape of the problem better than a permanent seat. If you want to pressure-test whether your problem is a leadership gap or a process gap, our note on [diagnosing a broken revenue engine](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-diagnostic-series-b) walks through the distinction.

The failure mode to avoid is hiring senior GTM leadership to escape a problem that's actually upstream — a weak ICP, a product that doesn't retain, or a pricing model that caps deal size. A fractional CRO will surface those truths quickly, but no revenue leader, fractional or full-time, can out-execute a broken funnel. Name the problem first.

## Fractional versus full-time: the real decision tree

The choice isn't binary between "cheap contractor" and "expensive executive." It's a sequence of gating questions about certainty, capital, and control. A full-time CRO is the right call when you know the exact motion you're scaling, you can afford the fully-loaded cost (typically $350K–$500K base plus equity plus a variable component), and the role demands day-to-day ownership and team management that a part-timer structurally can't provide. A fractional CRO wins when any of those three conditions is missing — when you're still discovering the motion, still building the case for the spend, or still short of the team size that justifies a full-time manager of managers.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Series B revenue leadership gap] --> B{Do you know the exact GTM motion to scale}
  B -->|No still discovering| C[Fractional CRO to define and prove the motion]
  B -->|Yes proven and repeatable| D{Can you fund a full loaded package now}
  D -->|Not yet| C
  D -->|Yes| E{Does the role need daily team ownership}
  E -->|Yes large team| F[Full time CRO]
  E -->|Not yet small team| C
  C --> G[Build operating system then transition to full time hire]
  G --> F
```

Read the tree as a filter, not a verdict. The overwhelming majority of Series B companies land in the fractional bucket for at least one honest reason, and that's fine — it's the *correct* answer for the stage, not a compromise. What the tree also makes clear is the destination: the fractional engagement almost always terminates in a full-time hire. You are not choosing fractional *instead of* full-time; you're choosing fractional *before* full-time so that the full-time hire lands on a foundation instead of a blank page. The mistake founders make is treating the two as competing philosophies rather than sequential phases. For a deeper look at how the two roles hand off cleanly, see our teardown of the [fractional-to-permanent transition plan](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-to-fulltime-cro-handoff).

There's also a subtler cost the tree doesn't show: the price of a bad full-time hire. Executive search fees run 25–33% of first-year cash comp, a mishired CRO typically isn't diagnosed for 6–9 months, and the cleanup — re-recruiting, re-org, lost quarters — can burn a year of runway. A fractional engagement is, among other things, an insurance policy against that outcome. It lets you validate the profile you actually need before you commit a board seat's worth of equity and a search firm's worth of cash to finding it.

## What does a fractional CRO cost, and how do the models differ?

Fractional CRO pricing is not standardized, and you should be skeptical of anyone who quotes a single number. The common structures are a monthly retainer for a fixed block of hours or days, a day-rate for episodic work, and — increasingly — a retainer plus a performance or equity component that aligns the operator to outcomes. Retainers commonly land in the $8K–$20K per month range depending on time commitment, market, and the operator's pedigree, with day-focused engagements (say, two days a week) sitting at the higher end. Equity-linked deals trade some cash for upside and signal that the operator believes in the company — but they also complicate the eventual transition, so structure them with a clear end date and a defined scope.

The honest way to evaluate cost is not "retainer versus salary" but *cost per unit of installed capability.* A full-time CRO at $400K all-in who spends their first two quarters ramping, building relationships, and learning your market may deliver less operating-system progress in six months than a fractional operator who's built this exact system five times and starts contributing in week two. The fractional premium per hour is real — you pay more for each hour because you're buying concentrated senior time — but the total spend to reach a working revenue system is frequently lower, because you're paying only for the hours that produce architecture and none of the hours that produce ramp.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Revenue leadership spend] --> B[Full time CRO]
  A --> C[Fractional CRO]
  B --> D[High fixed cost every month]
  B --> E[Long ramp before value]
  B --> F[Full team ownership]
  C --> G[Lower monthly cost]
  C --> H[Fast time to value]
  C --> I[Limited hours and no daily ownership]
  D --> J{Which matches your Series B constraints}
  G --> J
  H --> J
  I --> J
```

Watch three cost traps. First, scope creep: a retainer for "GTM strategy" that quietly expands into daily deal desk and rep coaching burns the operator's limited hours on work a director should do. Second, the permanent-fractional trap: month 14 of a fractional retainer usually means you've under-invested in owned leadership and are renting a seat that should now be full-time. Third, the two-hats problem: many fractional CROs run several clients, so verify their capacity honestly and write availability into the contract. The cheapest fractional CRO who's spread across six companies is more expensive than a focused one at twice the rate.

## How do you structure the engagement so it actually works?

A fractional CRO engagement fails on structure far more often than on talent. The single most important input is a written scope with a defined end state — not "help us grow revenue" but "in 120 days, deliver a documented sales process with stage exit criteria, a rebuilt comp plan, a board-grade forecast model, and hiring scorecards for two AEs and one sales manager." Deliverables, not vibes. The operator should own the *system*; your internal team should own *execution against it.* Blur that line and you get a very expensive individual contributor.

Set the cadence deliberately. A fractional CRO who parachutes in for a monthly board deck and disappears will never build trust with the reps whose behavior needs to change. Weekly working sessions with the sales team, a standing forecast review, and direct access to the founder or CEO are the minimum for the operator to function as a leader rather than a consultant. At the same time, protect their hours — route deal-desk questions and one-off asks to an internal owner so the senior time goes to architecture. The internal counterpart matters enormously: pair the fractional CRO with a rising sales manager or RevOps lead who absorbs the system and becomes the continuity when the engagement ends. That person is often your eventual VP of Sales, and the fractional CRO's real legacy is having built them.

Finally, define the exit at the *start.* The best engagements name the trigger for transition up front — a revenue milestone, a headcount threshold, or a fixed date — and the fractional CRO's mandate explicitly includes writing the scorecard for their own full-time replacement and helping you interview for it. An operator who's structurally incentivized to make the relationship permanent will, consciously or not, avoid making themselves unnecessary. The good ones want to work themselves out of a job, and they'll tell you so in the first meeting. Our [RevOps operating cadence guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-cadence) has the meeting and reporting rhythm we recommend installing during the engagement.

## When is a fractional CRO the wrong answer?

There are clear cases where fractional is a mistake. If you already have a repeatable, well-understood motion and a team of 25+ quota-carrying reps, you need an owner in the building every day — a fractional operator can't manage a sales org of that scale on two days a week, and trying to force it starves both the operator and the team. If your primary problem is execution intensity rather than architecture — you know exactly what to do and just need someone to drive it relentlessly through the org — a full-time leader with skin in the game will outperform a part-timer every time.

Fractional is also wrong when it's being used to avoid a decision. Some founders reach for a fractional CRO because committing to a full-time hire feels scary, and "fractional" lets them defer the choice. That's a legitimate use for a *defined window* — but if you find yourself renewing the retainer quarter after quarter with no transition plan, you've stopped buying architecture and started renting an excuse. The tell is that the operator is no longer building new systems; they're maintaining the ones they built, which is exactly the work a full-time hire should own. And finally, fractional is wrong when the real gap is upstream of go-to-market entirely — a retention problem, a pricing problem, a product problem. No revenue leader fixes those, and paying senior GTM rates to rediscover them is expensive. When in doubt, run the diagnostic before you run the search.

## Related questions

### How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?
Typically 10–25 hours, structured as one to three days a week or a fixed monthly block. The exact number should map to defined deliverables, not a round figure — architecture-heavy early phases justify more time than steady-state phases.

### Fractional CRO or VP of Sales for a Series B startup?
A VP of Sales runs the team and hits the number; a fractional CRO builds the system the VP executes. Many Series B companies need both — the fractional CRO installs the operating model, then hires and coaches the full-time VP who owns daily execution.

### Can a fractional CRO become a full-time CRO?
Sometimes, and it can be a clean path since they already know your business. But structure the fractional engagement to test that fit deliberately, and don't assume it — the skills to *build* a system differ from the skills to *run a large org* day to day.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run 6–12 months. Shorter than six rarely allows a full operating system to take hold; longer than twelve usually signals you've deferred a full-time hire you should have made. Define the end trigger at the start.

### What ARR range is a fractional CRO right for?
Commonly $2M–$20M ARR — past the founder-led phase but before the org is large enough to justify a full-time CRO with a deep bench. Series B companies frequently sit squarely in this band.

## FAQ

**What is a fractional CRO?**
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is an experienced go-to-market executive who works part-time across one or more companies, providing senior revenue leadership — strategy, process, comp design, forecasting, and hiring architecture — without the cost or commitment of a full-time hire.

**Is a fractional CRO worth it for a Series B company?**
For most, yes — provided the problem is genuinely a go-to-market leadership and process gap. The value comes from installing a repeatable revenue system quickly and de-risking the eventual full-time hire, not from the operator personally closing deals.

**How much does a fractional CRO cost?**
Structures vary widely: monthly retainers commonly fall in the $8K–$20K range, with day-rate and equity-linked models also common. Evaluate cost as spend-per-installed-capability, not just retainer-versus-salary, since ramp time on a full-time hire is a real hidden cost.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a consultant?**
A consultant advises and produces recommendations; a fractional CRO takes operational ownership of the revenue function — sitting in forecast reviews, coaching managers, and being accountable for the system working. The difference is embedded leadership versus external advice.

**Will a fractional CRO manage our sales team day to day?**
Not in the way a full-time leader does. They set the operating model, coach managers, and run key cadences, but daily deal-by-deal management should be owned by an internal manager or VP. Expecting daily team ownership from a part-time operator is a common structural mistake.

**How do we measure a fractional CRO's success?**
By installed system, not just short-term bookings: a documented sales process, a trustworthy forecast, a comp plan that drives the right behavior, hiring scorecards, and a capable internal successor. Bookings improve as the system takes hold, but the durable deliverable is the operating model.

**When should we transition from fractional to full-time?**
When the motion is proven, the team has grown past what part-time leadership can manage (often 15–25+ reps), and you can fund the full package. The fractional CRO should help define and hire their own replacement as part of the engagement.

**Can we hire a fractional CRO before Series B?**
Yes — some Series A companies use one to establish early GTM discipline. The engagement is usually lighter-touch and more strategy-focused at that stage, since there's less of a team and process to build on top of.
